content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, the lamb is overwhelmingly understood as a symbol of Jesus Christ as the innocent, sacrificial victim whose death atones for sin — the 'Lamb of God.' The image fuses the Passover lamb of the Exodus, the daily sacrificial lambs of the Levitical system, and the suffering servant led 'like a lamb to the slaughter,' all read typologically as fulfilled in Christ's crucifixion.", "primary_basis": ["John 1:29", "John 1:36", "Exodus 12:1-13 (the Passover lamb)", "Isaiah 53:7", "Acts 8:32-35", "1 Corinthians 5:7 ('Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed')", "1 Peter 1:18-19 ('a lamb without blemish or defect')", "Revelation 5:6-14", "Genesis 22:7-8 ('God himself will provide the lamb')", "Leviticus 1:10; 4:32 (lambs in the sacrificial system)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "The apocalyptic, conquering Lamb of Revelation: not merely a sacrificial victim but the enthroned, victorious ruler and judge — 'the Lamb who was slain' who wages war, opens the scroll, and reigns. Scholars treat this as a distinct (though related) symbolic register emphasizing paradoxical power through sacrifice.", "basis": ["Revelation 5:6-13", "Revelation 6:16 ('the wrath of the Lamb')", "Revelation 17:14 ('the Lamb will overcome them')", "Revelation 19:7-9 (marriage supper of the Lamb)", "Revelation 21:22-23"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Lambs/sheep as God's people — believers characterized as vulnerable, dependent members of the flock under the divine Shepherd or under pastoral care.", "basis": ["John 21:15 ('Feed my lambs')", "Isaiah 40:11", "Luke 10:3 ('I am sending you out like lambs among wolves')", "Psalm 100:3", "John 10 (shepherd/flock imagery)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The lamb as an emblem of innocence, meekness, gentleness, and non-retaliation more generally — a moral or character symbol rather than a strictly sacrificial one.", "basis": ["Isaiah 53:7 (silence before shearers)", "Jeremiah 11:19 ('a gentle lamb led to the slaughter')", "2 Samuel 12:1-6 (Nathan's parable of the ewe lamb)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The lamb in eschatological peace imagery — the wolf dwelling with the lamb as a picture of the restored, peaceable kingdom.", "basis": ["Isaiah 11:6", "Isaiah 65:25"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "A deceptive counterfeit: the second beast of Revelation has 'two horns like a lamb' but speaks like a dragon, using lamb imagery to symbolize false Christ-likeness or religious deception.", "basis": ["Revelation 13:11"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "History-of-religions or critical readings that ground the Revelation lamb in astrological (Aries), messianic-warrior-ram (e.g., 1 Enoch, Testament of Joseph), or other Second Temple Jewish traditions rather than primarily in sacrificial typology.", "basis": ["1 Enoch 89-90 (Animal Apocalypse)", "Testament of Joseph 19:8", "Scholarly literature on Revelation 5"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "The lamb is among the most stable and widely agreed symbols in Christian interpretation: Christ as the atoning sacrificial Lamb of God is affirmed across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions (reflected liturgically in the Agnus Dei) and in mainstream biblical scholarship as the intended New Testament typology. The alternative readings listed are largely complementary registers (conquering Lamb, flock imagery, innocence, eschatological peace) rather than rival definitions; genuine disagreement is mostly limited to scholarly debate over the precise background sources of the Revelation lamb and, in critical scholarship, over which Old Testament stream (Passover, Isaiah 53, cultic sacrifice, or apocalyptic ram) most controls John 1:29."}
